title: The Crossing of Names: History, Allegory, and the Binding of the Ancient Literary Field
creator: Sharks, Lee
description: An essay on names as operations in the ancient literary field: a name can identify a person and at the same time install a speaking position, carry an earlier text, assign an office or claim divine and political authority. It takes Philo's word πολυώνυμος, many-named, for the figure the field keeps producing. It separates three operations: many-namedness, transfer or restamping, and differentiated personation. It reads them through Catullus's Lesbia, Clodia and Cicero's restamped Liberty, Philo's renamings, Revelation's withheld names, Gellius's Sapphic banquet, and the Josephan witnesses. It aligns the original-language witnesses of the hedge from Sappho 31 and Catullus 51 to the Testimonium, the Slavonic War and the Acta Pilati. It traces the archive's phantom ei exestin to Whiston's 'if it be lawful'. Alternative identity maps are read as inventories of proposed crossings, tested relation by relation. The essay joins the archive's author-boundary protocols and leaves the direction of each cross-corpus seam open.
substrate: AI-assisted (substrate). By Lee Sharks. Draft 0.2 was prepared by ChatGPT under the author's direction from the conversation and a saved research checkpoint. Drafts 0.3–0.8 were prepared by Claude (Anthropic) under the author's direction, with reviews by DeepSeek and ChatGPT checked against the texts before entry.
methodology: Close reading in the original languages. Every primary locus is quoted from a seated text or an open edition, and the witness for each is given in the Original-language ledger. The Acta Pilati Greek was checked on Tischendorf's printed page (1876, p. 314). Identity proposals are decomposed into their constituent relations and tested against the archive's author-boundary protocols: the five admission conditions, the dependency protocol and the symmetric evaluation.
falsification_conditions: §9b's decision table states, for each proposed author boundary, what would show that the boundary does work. The Catullus–Josephus alignment is a recurrence of form, and its direction is open (#1602). The Revelation identification rests on three textual joins: the shared formula, καινόν with its recipient, and the speaker's titles. It fails if those joins are read otherwise.

wiki_article: The Crossing of Names: History, Allegory, and the Binding of the Ancient Literary Field is an essay by Lee Sharks, deposited as version 1.0 on 12 November 2026. It treats a name as an operation. A name can identify a person while it installs a speaking position, carries an earlier text, assigns an office or claims divine and political authority. It takes Philo's word πολυώνυμος, many-named, which he gives to both Moses and the Logos, for the figure the field keeps producing. It separates three operations: many-namedness, transfer or restamping (Philo's μεταχαράττειν), and differentiated personation. The essay reads these operations across Catullus's Lesbia, Clodia and the Liberty Cicero contests in De domo sua, Philo's renamings, the withheld names of Revelation 2:17, 3:12 and 19:12, and Gellius's Sapphic banquet with the Plato epigram two chapters on. It aligns the original-language witnesses of the hedge on naming a man from Sappho 31 and Catullus 51 through the Testimonium, the Slavonic War and the Acta Pilati. It traces the archive's earlier phantom ei exestin to Whiston's English 'if it be lawful'. It reads alternative identity maps as inventories of proposed crossings, tested relation by relation, and joins the archive's author-boundary protocols. The direction of each cross-corpus seam is left open.
